name: revocable-forwarder
intent: Let a collaborator use an object through a forwarding wrapper that the grantor can switch off at any time through a separate control, so authority already handed out can be withdrawn without destroying the target and without the collaborator's cooperation.
problem: A capability is just a reference, so once a collaborator has been given access to an object there is no built-in way to take it back: the grantor can destroy the object, ask the collaborator to stop, or leave the access standing. The recurring decision is how to grant access that is bounded in time - temporary use of a file, a service object, a session, an account - while keeping a control that only the grantor holds.
context: Object-capability settings, and any in-process design in which authority travels as references rather than as a global identity: plugin and extension hosts lending a service object to foreign code, multi-tenant object graphs giving a worker one tenant-scoped resource, session-scoped services, and capability-based workflow or financial systems in which a grant must be provably withdrawn. It applies when the grantor keeps its own reference to the target and can intercept every call through the reference it handed out; where the runtime lets references be forged, dereferenced around the wrapper or reached by reflection, marshalling or FFI, the same structure degrades from an enforcement mechanism to a discipline.
benefits: Revocation where the platform has none: a capability cannot be taken back because the reference is the authority, so the wrapper supplies the missing undo without changing the target or the runtime.
Temporal least authority: access is granted for a bounded period - a session, a workflow step, a plugin run - and withdrawn at the end instead of standing until the process exits.
No cooperation required: the collaborator keeps its code unchanged and simply receives the wrapper instead of the target, so withdrawal is unilateral and unannounced.
One control point per grant: the revoker is a separate, small object that only the grantor keeps, which makes withdrawal an explicit and auditable operation rather than a hunt for references.
The target stays unaware and unrebuilt: nothing is added to the protected object and revocation does not destroy it, so other legitimate holders of the target are unaffected.

Revocation can be scoped or drained: because the wrapper owns the call path, revocation can fail fast for new calls, wait for in-flight calls (drain), or be tied to a lexical scope such as a with block.
tradeoffs: Revocation is only as complete as the reference discipline around it: the wrapper stops forwarding, it does not make the target unreachable, so a second reference, an ambient route or a target returned from a call keeps working - the narrower forwarder cannot revoke reachability, which is why membranes exist.

Check-and-forward must be one atomic step: if the enable state is read across an asynchronous or distributed boundary, a call can pass the check and still be forwarded after revocation has returned (the documented check-then-forward race).

In-flight calls have no universally correct policy: immediate revocation lets calls already past the check complete, while draining couples revocation latency to the slowest call and one blocked call can stall revocation indefinitely.

Queued or remote call paths can delay and reorder the revocation itself, so withdrawal is only as prompt as the transport; the delayed-toggle scenario is a documented denial-of-service vector unless the revoker acts locally.

Every grant costs an indirection plus two objects (forwarder and revoker), and the wrapper changes identity at the boundary: equality, hashing, type tests and debug output see the wrapper rather than the target.
Interface drift: the forwarder mirrors the target's interface, so a new method means revisiting every wrapper, and any member that is forwarded without the check silently stays unrevokable.

Lifetime coupling and leaks: wrappers that outlive their purpose keep forwarding, and a wrapper holding the target strongly keeps it alive after revocation, so weak references or an explicit release step are needed.

participants.responsibility: Creates the forwarder and the revocation control, hands out only the forwarder, and keeps the control plus any other reference to the target.
Implements the target's interface, checks the enable state on every call and either forwards to the target or fails; after revocation it never reaches the target.
The protected object whose authority is being lent; it is unaware of the delegation and is neither modified nor destroyed by revocation.
The mutable state the forwarder consults; in the corrected form it lives inside the forwarding gate so that the check and the forward happen in one step instead of across two messages.
The control object that flips the enable state; it is handed only to the grantor, and flipping it is the revocation event.
The party that receives the forwarder and uses the capability; it never needs to cooperate to be cut off, and normally never sees the target.

use_cases: A plugin or extension host lends a file, network or service object to foreign code and revokes it when the plugin is unloaded or breaches policy.
A multi-tenant worker receives one tenant-scoped resource for the duration of a job and loses it at job end, without the tenant object being torn down.
Session teardown in a long-lived server: the handler works through the wrapper, and logout revokes future calls before the session's resources are freed.
Capability-based workflow and financial systems that give an agent temporary authority over an account or a document and revoke it when the task completes.
Temporary elevated access for maintenance or debugging, where the requirement is to show that the extra authority has provably ended (audit evidence).
Graceful decommissioning of a shared resource: revoke new work through the wrapper, drain the calls already in flight, then release the resource.

The Scala ocaps framework's Revocable/Caretaker API returns a proxied capability plus a private Revoker, so a session, logout, timeout or supervisor can make later calls fail without changing the target.

JavaScript's standard Proxy.revocable() and the Chrome Extensions chrome.permissions API provide browser/runtime counterparts: keep the revoke/remove control private, and do not mistake the platform wrapper or permission record for protection against an already leaked target reference.

AWS IAM role-session revocation for temporary STS credentials is a distributed analogue of withdrawing a forwarded grant: policy evaluation denies subsequent requests, but propagation and credential caching mean it is not the atomic in-process check-and-forward gate described here.
avoid_when: The restriction to enforce is attenuation (read-only, quota), not withdrawal: an attenuating forwarder is simpler and equally effective against an honest collaborator.
Every reference into a subsystem must lose access together, including references exchanged through the interface: use a membrane, of which the revocable membrane forwarder combines both.
The other party shares the process and must actually be confined: a process, VM, seccomp or WebAssembly boundary is stronger than an in-process wrapper that reflection or FFI can bypass.
The collaborator legitimately owns the object for its whole lifetime: revocability buys nothing and the wrapper only adds indirection - hand over the target or pass a narrower interface instead.
The grant can be avoided by scoping: narrowing the interface, passing a copy, or restructuring lifetimes often removes the need to undo access at all.
anti_patterns: Handing out the forwarder and the revoker together, or letting the collaborator reach the revoker, so revocation becomes cooperative and access can be re-enabled by the wrong party.

Checking the enable flag and forwarding as two steps, or reading the flag across an asynchronous or network boundary: the documented check-then-forward race lets a call pass the check and still be forwarded after revocation.
Revoking by dropping the reference or deleting the target instead of flipping state: copies handed out earlier keep working, and destroying the target revokes every legitimate holder at once.
A forwarder that leaks the target - a method returning itself, an unwrapped accessor, identity-revealing debug output, a reflective escape - so the collaborator bypasses the wrapper.

Calling the wrapper complete mediation while the collaborator also holds an ambient route to the target (a global registry, a service locator, another capability): revoking one reference revokes nothing.
Promoting or re-exporting the target's whole interface (interface embedding, wildcard delegation, export clauses) without mediating each member, so the unmediated members stay live after revocation.
design_principles: Least authority bounded in time: lend the smallest capability that does the job and make its withdrawal an explicit event.
Separation of use from control: the collaborator holds the capability to use, the grantor keeps the capability to revoke, and neither can act with the other's authority.
Complete mediation over the references you hand out: every call through the forwarder is checked, and no unmediated alias of the target leaves the grantor.
Fail-safe default: after revocation every path denies rather than attempting a best-effort forward.
Single responsibility per role: the forwarder checks and forwards, the gate holds and flips the state, the target does the work.
best_practices: Fold the enable state into the forwarding gate so that check-and-forward is one uninterruptible step; never read the flag from a separate object first (the repair in the cited analysis is exactly this refactor).

Decide and document the in-flight policy: deny calls that start after revocation and let those already past the check finish, or drain with an exclusive lock when revocation must wait for running calls.
Keep the revoker local to the grantor, hand it to no one else, and make revocation one-way; if re-enabling is a feature, model it as an explicit enable operation rather than a blind toggle.
Never return, expose or describe the target through the forwarder: no self-returning methods, no unwrapped accessors, no reflective or debug escape hatch.
Mediate the interface explicitly and fail closed for anything unmediated: an unknown member should raise rather than silently forward, or be deliberately documented as unrevokable.

Watch lifetimes: hold the target weakly where revocation should end its life, revoke before releasing the target, and prefer a per-grant wrapper over a shared instance whose revocation is all-or-nothing.
sources: D. D. Redell, Naming and Protection in Extendable Operating Systems (PhD thesis, University of California, Berkeley, 1974; published as Project MAC Technical Report TR-140, MIT) - the original caretaker pattern: a forwarder between two parties whose access the third party can revoke.

Deian Stefan & John C. Mitchell, Analysing Object-Capability Patterns With Murphi (2011), section 2.2.1 (the revocable forwarder as Redell's caretaker pattern: enable slot, gate and forwarder), section 3.3.2 (the no-forwarding-post-revocation invariant), section 4.1.2 (the check-then-forward TOCTTOU trace and the delayed-toggle trace) and section 4.2.1 with Listing 3 (the forwarding-gate repair, verified over 13,720,000 states) - the catalog's cited source for the Revocable Forwarder / Caretaker row.

Toby Murray, Analysing Object-Capability Security (FCS-ARSPA-WITS 2008), section 3.1 - the RevocableMembrane analysis, whose FDR counterexample is the same check-then-forward race in a concurrent object-capability context.

Mark S. Miller, Robust Composition: Towards a Unified Approach to Access Control and Concurrency Control (PhD thesis, Johns Hopkins University, 2006) - the object-capability account of revocation, cited by both analyses above.
